title: The Best Natural Lifter You've NEVER Heard Of (Hersovyac)
summary: NH profiles Hersovyac, a little-known French natural lifter with a Silver Era physique (5'7, 180 lb lean, 19-inch neck, 28-inch waist) who trains full body three times a week with heavy low-rep, high-set vertical presses and weighted pull-ups, heavy neck work and minimal chest and legs. He breaks down three sessions, extracts lessons on prioritisation, supersets and building work capacity, warns that the split is too specialised to copy, and grades the physique.
claims: Hersovyac has trained since 2013 after swimming and martial arts, and transformed steadily over 10 years following Silver Era methods
At 5'7 and 180 lb lean (10-12% body fat) Hersovyac has 17 in arms, 44 in chest, 28 in waist, 24 in legs and a 19 in neck
NH is convinced Hersovyac is natural based on his steady progression and physique
Silver Era lifters trained full body three times a week; two full body sessions are not enough, three is perfect, four is too much
Partial-range behind-the-neck press (stopping behind the head) trades range of motion for load safely, avoiding impingement
Doing face pulls or band pull-aparts for 20-25 reps between pressing sets is smart for shoulder health and mobility
The muscles with the most work capacity and strength in a physique tend to be the biggest
Slingshot weighted dips deload the bottom and shoulder, skewing the work to triceps
Cheat-style T-bar rows are mostly a hip hinge and work legs, posterior chain and yoke more than lats
A full body does not have to train everything equally; skew it toward your priorities
Vertical presses pair beautifully with vertical pulls, horizontal with horizontal
Using heavy and light days (different rep ranges) on a favourite lift varies intensity and volume without changing the lift, enabling longer progress
A 10x10 on chest-supported rows works because the lower back is not taxed; on barbell rows it would be idiotic
Order presses from most to least shoulder-taxing so many sets can be done relatively safely
Horizontal presses destroy shoulders more than vertical presses because of the scapula angle
There is no perfect push-pull ratio, but if you press a lot you must pull roughly as much or you'll get rounded shoulders and injuries
Naturals can recover from large volume with proper exercise selection, intensity and frequency management; he trains six days a week, two hours a day
Program as a pyramid: the most strenuous exercises at the top of the session, easier ones like arm isolation later
Being strong and resilient on isolation and doing lots of volume on it is how you beat the spider physique
Not everyone wants huge legs; it is fine to train legs minimally, once a week, if your goal is a big upper body
Snatch-grip block pulls add upper back and yoke stimulus within leg work
Superset neck work with leg exercises; neck extensions and neck curls are underrated
Hersovyac does neck curls with two 45 lb plates for 30 reps because he trains the neck constantly
Deficit handstand push-ups are probably the best bodyweight shoulder exercise
French presses with the upper back rounded over a preacher bench recruit triceps more and may relieve pain from the movement
Big shoulders come from heavy presses, not spamming lateral raises; raises should come after the compounds
Don't copy Hersovyac's split: too much pressing and vertical pulling volume, too little chest and legs for most; copy his mindset and arm training
Pairing low reps with high set counts gives both high intensity and high volume, but needs muscular endurance; back-off sets and drop sets help
Static rep ranges invite sandbagging, but they may suit some lifters
He would open sessions with legs because he wants big legs; prioritise according to the physique you want
Progressive overload is not only weight on the bar but also more reps and more sets; a bigger muscle is stronger and also more enduring
The neck grows with the traps, so pairing them makes sense; a neck should match the jawline
Pull-ups make up 70-80% of Hersovyac's back volume and he has the best upper back NH has seen: pull-ups build the upper back
The upper back can handle huge volume; most people can reach 60-70% of Hersovyac's
Strong extensions behind the head build the triceps
A short biceps insertion limits how impressive the biceps looks
Fat-grip work across pulls and curls skews work toward the forearms, helped by long forearm muscle insertions
Many prefer a flatter chest with dominant shoulders; as shoulders grow they steal more work from the chest on horizontal presses
Knee injuries and weak tendons can leave a muscle like the quads stuck as a weak point
Pulling from blocks deloads hamstrings, glutes and lower back
Big glutes are an injury insurance policy and key for longevity
Abs and calves developed through past sports can be maintained with minimal work; if you were inactive, you must train them
NH's waist is 36 inches and his neck about 17.5 inches
NH uses 85-90 kg on dumbbell French presses for 8-12 reps
exercises: stop behind head, no deep flexion
upper back without lower back fatigue
round upper back over preacher pad
